\begin{abstract}

Cardiovascular disease risk is a cumulative result of biological, behavioral, and demographic factors, with Body Mass Index (BMI) serving as a useful but imperfect indicator of underlying health and risk patterns. This study examines how race, sex, age, pre-existing health conditions, and behavior (such as smoking and alcohol consumption) relate to BMI and the probability of of experiencing an heart attack. Multiple linear regression was performed to investigate the factors involved in BMI, while a logistic regression model was fit to determine how predictors impacted the odds of heart disease. Overall, we found that....**TBD MLR results**. The logistic regression model revealed that individuals with the greatest odds of experiencing heart disease were over 55 years old, White, and female. Medical conditions such as stroke, kidney disease, diabetes, skin cancer, asthma, and difficulty walking also significantly (p < 0.05) increased the risk of heart attack. On the other hand, this risk significantly (p < 0.05) decreased for those with goold health and, unexpectedly, those who consumed alcohol.

\end{abstract}
